# `silk/geometry/affine`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Two-dimensional affine transforms: scale, rotation, skew, and translation in one matrix.

## When to use
Use [`Affine2`](#Affine2) to move, scale, rotate, or skew points, vectors, and rectangles in a plane, such
as an SVG `transform` attribute, a font matrix, or a canvas transform. Use
`silk.geometry.matrix` for projective (3x3) and three-dimensional (4x4) transforms.

## Details
An affine transform is a `Copy` struct with six public coefficients, generic over its number
type `T`. It maps a point `(x, y)` to `(xx * x + xy * y + dx, yx * x + yy * y + dy)`. The
coefficient order `xx, yx, xy, yy, dx, dy` is the order of SVG and CSS `matrix(a, b, c, d, e,
f)`, of PDF, and of the OpenType and FreeType font matrices, so [`fromCoefficients`](#Affine2.impl.fromCoefficients) takes those
six numbers as written.

`left * right` composes two transforms: the result applies `right` first, then `left`. So a list
of transforms written left to right, as in SVG, multiplies in the written order. `transform *
point` maps a `silk.geometry.point.Point2`, and `transform * vector` maps a
`silk.geometry.vector.Vector2` without the translation. `&a == &b` compares all six coefficients
when `T: Equal`.

## Gotchas
[`rotation`](#Affine2.impl.rotation) and [`skew`](#Affine2.impl.skew) take radians. A positive angle turns the positive x axis toward
positive y, which is clockwise in a y-down space such as SVG and counterclockwise in a y-up
space such as a font.

## Examples
### Rotate around a point
```silk
import silk.geometry.affine { Affine2 }
import silk.geometry.point { Point2 }
import silk.geometry.vector { Vector2 }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let pivot = Vector2<f64>.new(10.0, 0.0)
  let turn = Affine2<f64>.translation(pivot) * Affine2<f64>.rotation(3.141592653589793)
    * Affine2<f64>.translation(-pivot)
  let moved = turn * Point2<f64>.new(12.0, 0.0)
  if moved.x < 7.999999 || moved.x > 8.000001 || moved.y < -0.000001 || moved.y > 0.000001 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `Affine2` with `import silk.geometry.affine { Affine2 }`.

## `Affine2`

```silk
pub struct Affine2<T>
```

A two-dimensional affine transform with coefficients of number type `T`.

### When to use

Use `Affine2` for any combination of scale, rotation, skew, reflection, and translation in a
plane.

### Details

The transform maps `(x, y)` to `(xx * x + xy * y + dx, yx * x + yy * y + dy)`. As a matrix that
multiplies a column vector, it is `[xx xy dx; yx yy dy; 0 0 1]`. The field order matches SVG and
CSS `matrix(a, b, c, d, e, f)`: `a = xx`, `b = yx`, `c = xy`, `d = yy`, `e = dx`, and `f = dy`.

`left * right` applies `right` first, then `left`. `transform * point` maps a `Point2<T>`, and
`transform * vector` maps a `Vector2<T>` with no translation. `&a == &b` compares all six
coefficients when `T: Equal`.

<a id="Affine2.impl.rotation"></a>

### Associated function `rotation`

```silk
pub fn rotation(radians: T) -> Affine2<T>
```

Returns the transform that rotates by `radians` around the origin.

#### Details

A positive angle turns the positive x axis toward positive y. That is clockwise in a y-down
space such as SVG, where it matches `rotate(angle)` after a degree-to-radian conversion.

<a id="Affine2.impl.skew"></a>

### Associated function `skew`

```silk
pub fn skew(x: T, y: T) -> Affine2<T>
```

Returns the transform that skews by `x` radians along the x axis and `y` radians along the y
axis.

#### Details

The result is `[1, tan(y), tan(x), 1, 0, 0]`. `skew(angle, 0)` is SVG `skewX(angle)` and
`skew(0, angle)` is SVG `skewY(angle)`, after a degree-to-radian conversion.

<a id="Affine2.impl.determinant"></a>

### Method `determinant`

```silk
pub fn determinant(self: Self) -> T
```

Returns `xx * yy - yx * xy`, the factor by which the transform scales area.

#### Details

A negative determinant means the transform reflects. Zero means it is singular: it flattens
the plane onto a line or a point and has no inverse.

<a id="Affine2.impl.inverse"></a>

### Method `inverse`

```silk
pub fn inverse(self: Self) -> Option<Affine2<T>>
```

Returns the transform that undoes `self`, or `None` when `self` has no finite inverse.

#### Details

`None` means `self` is singular or has an infinite or NaN coefficient, or that the inverse has
an infinite or NaN coefficient. Each row is scaled by its largest coefficient before the
determinant is formed, so a valid transform with very large or very small scales does not
overflow or underflow to a false `None`. No epsilon rejects a small but invertible scale.

<a id="Affine2.impl.maxScale"></a>

### Method `maxScale`

```silk
pub fn maxScale(self: Self) -> T
```

Returns the largest factor by which the transform stretches any vector.

#### When to use

Use `maxScale` to convert a tolerance in device space to user space, such as a
curve-flattening tolerance or a stroke width.

#### Details

The result is the largest singular value of the linear part `[xx xy; yx yy]`; the translation
does not count. A transform with an infinite or NaN linear coefficient gives NaN or infinity.

<a id="Affine2.impl.transformRect"></a>

### Method `transformRect`

```silk
pub fn transformRect(self: Self, bounds: Rect<T>) -> Rect<T>
```

Returns the smallest rectangle that holds the four transformed corners of `bounds`.

#### Details

The result holds the whole transformed rectangle, because an affine transform maps a rectangle
to a parallelogram whose corners are the transformed corners. For a rotated or skewed
transform it is larger than the transformed shape. To bound a curve exactly, transform the
curve first and bound the result.

#### Gotchas

An infinite or NaN coefficient or edge can give NaN edges. Test with `Rect.isFinite`.

<a id="Affine2.impl.isFinite"></a>

### Method `isFinite`

```silk
pub fn isFinite(self: Self) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when all six coefficients are neither infinite nor NaN.
